# Runtime Enforcement for Agents: Tetragon, OpenTelemetry, and nono

Put production tools in charge of the sandbox. Write Tetragon policies that observe, then kill, a coding agent's credential reads and outbound connections; route every event through an OpenTelemetry collector; then confine the same agent with nono so the paths and ports it may not touch stop existing at all.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

This lab runs its agent on a local Ollama model. The Zenable sandbox has the model already downloaded and built; take the hosted version at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme.

**Duration** 45 minutes · **Difficulty** Advanced

**Topics** `Security` · `Guardrails & Policy` · `Observability`

**Prerequisites**

- The Syscalls and seccomp lab and the eBPF from scratch lab, or equivalent familiarity with system calls and eBPF hooks
- Docker and git
- Comfort reading YAML and JSON
- A Linux kernel 6.7 or newer with BTF. Your sandbox has one; the Getting started section checks

---

_This README is only the hands-on lab. The concept walk-through (You wouldn't ship the program you wrote last time · Terminology · Putting it together · Conclusion) lives on the [Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme)._

## Getting started

_~5 min · Hands-on_

Clone the rig and check the kernel. Tetragon needs BTF; nono's port filtering needs Landlock ABI 4, which is kernel 6.7:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement
uv sync --locked
uname -r
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm; echo
ls -la /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux
```

$ git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \

The agent is the same as the previous two labs: goose driving a local `qwen3-nothink` model through a three-step task that reads a decoy credential file and fetches a URL. Your sandbox built the model when it started. If you're continuing from either lab, goose is already here too. If not, open the panel:

<details>
<summary>Install goose</summary>

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/releases/download/stable/download_cli.sh | CONFIGURE=false GOOSE_VERSION=v1.46.0 bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

The [Syscalls and seccomp](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=syscalls-and-seccomp&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme) lab explains what each line does.

</details>

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
goose --version
ollama run qwen3-nothink "Reply with only the word: pong"
```

```console
$ export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
$ goose --version
 1.46.0
$ ollama run qwen3-nothink "Reply with only the word: pong"
pong
```

Tetragon matches processes by the absolute path of their binary, and goose lives under your home directory, so the policies ship as templates. Render them for this machine, then start Tetragon and the collector:

```bash
./scripts/render-policies.sh
docker compose up -d --wait
./scripts/wait-for-tetragon.sh
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
```

```console
$ ./scripts/render-policies.sh
rendered 10-observe.yaml for /home/rocky/.local/bin/goose
rendered 20-enforce.yaml for /home/rocky/.local/bin/goose
$ docker compose up -d --wait
$ ./scripts/wait-for-tetragon.sh
tetragon is answering
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
ID   NAME            STATE     FILTERID   NAMESPACE   SENSORS          KERNELMEMORY   MODE      NPOST   NENFORCE   NMONITOR
2    agent-observe   loading   0          (global)    generic_kprobe   0 B            unknown   0       0          0
```

Two containers, and a short wait: `compose up --wait` returns when the container is running, which for Tetragon is a few seconds before its programs are loaded and its API answers. Tetragon runs privileged with the host's pid namespace and this kernel's BTF mounted in, which is what it needs to attach to the same hooks you attached to by hand. The collector tails the JSON export file Tetragon writes. One policy is loaded, the observe one; the enforce one sits rendered beside it until we add it by hand.

## Observe

_~7 min · Hands-on_

Open `policies/10-observe.yaml.tmpl`. It hooks two kernel functions, and both times the selector starts by scoping to goose and everything goose spawns:

```yaml
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: security_file_permission
    syscall: false
    return: true
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: file
    - index: 1
      type: int   # 0x04 is MAY_READ, 0x02 is MAY_WRITE
    selectors:
    - matchBinaries:
      - operator: In
        followChildren: true
        values:
        - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
      matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: Postfix
        values:
        - "/.aws/credentials"
      - index: 1
        operator: Equal
        values:
        - "4"
  - call: tcp_connect
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: sock
    selectors:
    - matchBinaries:
      - operator: In
        followChildren: true
        values:
        - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
```

Compare this to last lab's C. `followChildren: true` is the `ProcessTree` you wrote, `type: file` is `bpf_d_path`, and `Postfix` on the path is the credential scan. `security_file_permission` is an LSM hook that runs on every read and write with the file already resolved, which is why the policy can match a path rather than a syscall argument. `tcp_connect` is the kernel function under every outbound TCP connection, with the socket decoded so the destination is right there.

Start reading events in a second terminal. `-o compact` is one line per event:

```bash
docker compose exec tetragon tetra getevents -o compact
```

Back in the first terminal, run the agent:

```bash
./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
```

Your second terminal fills up as it runs. The lines that matter:

```console
$ grep -E '📚 read|🔌 connect' tetra.out | head -10
```

Success! A `read` of the credentials by `cat`, with goose as the ancestor that makes it match, and a `connect` from `curl` to port 443 plus the model calls to `127.0.0.1:11434`. Nothing from any other process on the machine, because `matchBinaries` filtered in the kernel before the event was ever written.

Question: the policy watches `security_file_permission` rather than the `openat` syscall you hooked last lab. What does that buy, and what does it cost? Have a guess before opening the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

It buys the path. A syscall hook sees whatever string the caller passed, so `../../decoys/.aws/credentials` and a symlink both dodge a match on the literal path; the LSM hook sees the resolved file. It also fires on every read, not just the open, so a file descriptor handed across a fork is still caught. The cost is volume: `security_file_permission` fires for every read on the machine, and Tetragon's in-kernel filtering is the only reason that's affordable. A policy with a weak selector on this hook is how you learn what "eBPF overhead" means.

</details>

## Enforce

_~8 min · Hands-on_

`policies/20-enforce.yaml.tmpl` is the observe policy with one block added to each hook. The credential read gets a `Sigkill`, and the connect gets one too, but only for destinations off loopback, so the model on `127.0.0.1:11434` stays reachable:

```yaml
matchArgs:
- index: 0
  operator: NotDAddr
  values:
  - 127.0.0.0/8
  - ::1/128
matchActions:
- action: Sigkill
```

That's the rule seccomp couldn't express in the first lab, in four lines. Swap the policies: remove observe, add enforce. Tetragon loads and unloads them live:

```bash
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-observe
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
```

```console
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-observe
tracing policy "agent-observe" deleted
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
tracing policy "/policies/20-enforce.yaml" added
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
ID   NAME            STATE     FILTERID   NAMESPACE   SENSORS          KERNELMEMORY   MODE      NPOST   NENFORCE   NMONITOR
3    agent-enforce   enabled   0          (global)    generic_kprobe   765.46 kB      enforce   0       0          0
```

Run the agent again with the event stream open in the other terminal:

```bash
./run-agent.sh > agent-enforce.out 2>&1
```

```console
$ grep -E '📚 read|🔌 connect|💥 exit' tetra-enforce.out | head -10
```

Two `💥 exit … SIGKILL` lines: `cat` died on the credential read and `curl` died on the connect. goose itself carried on, reported both steps as failed, and its model calls to loopback went through untouched. One policy, kernel-enforced, that names the file and the destination.

Now the caveat you already know from last lab. `Sigkill` is a signal, and the read that triggered it had already returned by the time the signal landed. Look at what `cat` managed to print into goose's transcript:

```bash
grep -c DECOY agent-enforce.out || true
```

```console
0
```

Sometimes zero, sometimes one, depending on whether `cat` wrote its output before the signal arrived. Tetragon's docs are direct about this: `Sigkill` "does not always stop the operation being performed by the process that triggered the operation", and the fix is to pair it with an `Override` action, which uses the kernel's error injection to make the hooked function return an error before it runs. That works on security hooks and system calls, on kernels built with `CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE`. Add it to the credential selector:

```yaml
matchActions:
- action: Override
  argError: -1
- action: Sigkill
```

<details>
<summary>Try it</summary>

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("policies/rendered/20-enforce.yaml")
text = p.read_text()
marker = "      matchActions:\n      - action: Sigkill\n  - call: tcp_connect"
assert marker in text
p.write_text(text.replace(marker, "      matchActions:\n      - action: Override\n        argError: -1\n      - action: Sigkill\n  - call: tcp_connect"))
EOF
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-enforce
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
./run-agent.sh > agent-override.out 2>&1
grep -c DECOY agent-override.out || true
```

Zero, every time: the read returned `EPERM` and never produced bytes to print. The kernel decided instead of reacting, exactly the LSM hook you wrote by hand, expressed as two lines of YAML.

</details>

## The pipeline

_~6 min · Hands-on_

Everything `tetra getevents` showed you also went to a JSON file, and the collector has been tailing it the whole time. Its config parses each line and stamps the event kind as an attribute:

```yaml
file_log/tetragon:
  include: [/var/log/tetragon/tetragon.log]
  operators:
    - type: json_parser
      parse_to: attributes
    - type: add
      field: attributes.tetragon.event
      value: 'EXPR(keys(attributes)[0])'
```

Read the collector's output for the kill:

```bash
docker compose logs collector > collector.log 2>&1
grep -c 'LogRecord #' collector.log
grep -A20 'process_kprobe' collector.log | grep -E 'binary|SIGKILL|dport' | sed -n '1,8p'
```

The same events, now as log records with attributes, with `service.name: tetragon` on the resource. Beside them sit the records from last lab's hand-written watcher, if you left that collector running, and the two streams describe the same facts with the same vocabulary. Point the `debug` exporter at an OTLP backend and this is a real feed.

<details>
<summary>Stretch: trace the agent's model calls with zero code</summary>

[OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/) attaches to a running process from outside and emits HTTP spans without touching its code. `compose.yaml` carries it under a profile, targeting the goose binary and exporting to the same collector:

```bash
docker compose --profile obi up -d --wait
./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
docker compose logs obi > obi.log 2>&1
grep -E 'POST /api' obi.log | head -5
```

Each goose turn is a `POST /api/chat` span to Ollama, with duration, status and the peer, next to the kernel events for the same process. That's the model layer and the kernel layer in one stream, which is where an agent's story actually lives.

</details>

## nono

_~10 min · Hands-on_

Tetragon watches and reacts. nono restricts first. Install it, pinned and checksum-verified:

```bash
./scripts/install-nono.sh
```

```console
nono-v0.77.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz: OK
nono 0.77.0
```

Before running anything, ask nono what it would grant. `--dry-run -v` prints the Landlock ruleset and the ABI level the kernel offers:

```bash
nono run --dry-run -v --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh > dry-run.txt 2>&1
grep -E 'Landlock|net |ipc |zenable-labs' dry-run.txt
```

```console
$ nono run --dry-run -v --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh > dry-run.txt 2>&1
$ grep -E 'Landlock|net |ipc |zenable-labs' dry-run.txt
   r+w  /home/rocky/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/dry-run.txt (file) [group:system_read_linux_core]
   r+w  /home/rocky/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement (dir) [user]
   net  outbound blocked
   ipc  localhost:11434
   scope  Landlock V6 detected
2026-09-16T08:40:11.605594Z  INFO Landlock available (Landlock V6, features: Basic filesystem access control, File rename across directories (Refer), File truncation (Truncate), TCP network filtering, Device ioctl filtering, Signal and abstract UNIX socket scoping)
```

`Landlock V6 detected` means every rule can be applied on this kernel. The grants are the checkout, read-write, plus the system paths every process needs; the network is blocked and one localhost port is opened back up, 11434, for the model. Nothing else exists. Now the agent for real:

```bash
nono run --no-rollback --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

```console
$ nono run --no-rollback --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

Hmm, the credential read went through. `--allow "$PWD"` granted the whole checkout, and `decoys/` is inside it. That's the first thing to understand about a path allowlist: it's exactly as good as the paths you list. nono has a default deny list for the usual credential locations under your home directory, but a decoy inside the working directory isn't on it. And the fetch failed, this time not with a refused connection: with Landlock the socket can't be created towards that destination at all, so `curl` reports the failure at the network layer before any packet leaves.

Use the profile in the rig instead. It grants `workspace/` and `goose/` and never mentions `decoys/`, blocks the network and opens only port 11434, and passes only the home, executable path, locale and terminal settings into the child. Our model runs locally, so it needs none of the cloud credentials a shared coding agent sandbox may export. Landlock is an allow-list, so there is no denying a path inside a directory you granted; the checkout is granted piece by piece and the decoys are what's left out. The paths assume the checkout is under `$HOME/zenable-labs`; adjust them if yours lives elsewhere:

```jsonc
{
  "meta": {
    "name": "agent",
    "description": "goose, confined to the lab checkout and its local model"
  },
  "filesystem": {
    "read": ["$HOME/.local/bin"],
    "read_file": ["$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/run-agent.sh"],
    "allow": [
      "$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/workspace",
      "$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/goose"
    ]
  },
  "network": {
    "block": true,
    "open_port": [11434]
  },
  "environment": {
    "allow_vars": ["HOME", "PATH", "LANG", "TERM"]
  }
}
```

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/nono/profiles
cp nono/agent.jsonc ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono profile validate ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono why --profile agent --path "$PWD/decoys/.aws/credentials" --op read
nono why --profile agent --host example.com --port 443
```

```console
$ mkdir -p ~/.config/nono/profiles
$ cp nono/agent.jsonc ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
$ nono profile validate ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono profile: validating /home/rocky/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc

  [ok]  JSON syntax valid
  [ok]  All 18 group references valid

  Result: valid
$ nono why --profile agent --path "$PWD/decoys/.aws/credentials" --op read
DENIED
  Reason: path_not_granted
  Details: Path is not covered by any capability: /home/rocky/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/decoys/.aws/credentials
  Suggested fix: --read-file /home/rocky/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/decoys/.aws/credentials
$ nono why --profile agent --host example.com --port 443
DENIED
  Reason: network_blocked
  Details: Network access is fully blocked. Connection to example.com:443 would be denied.
  Suggested fix: --allow-domain example.com
```

`nono why` answers the policy question without running anything, which is the tool you want when a profile grows past a screen. Now the agent under the profile. `--workdir` tells nono where the agent runs, since a profile carries no working directory of its own:

```bash
nono run --no-rollback --profile agent --workdir "$PWD" -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

```console
$ nono run --no-rollback --profile agent --workdir "$PWD" -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

Success! `cat` got `Permission denied` on the credentials, `curl` couldn't even resolve example.com, and goose still talked to its model. No race, no signal, no event to react to, because from inside the sandbox those two things were never possible. And nono kept a record:

```bash
nono audit list --command run-agent.sh | head -8
```

```console
$ nono audit list --command run-agent.sh | head -8
```

The Python wrapper reads the same environment allowlist from the profile, with environment inheritance disabled. `nono_agent.py` builds the capability set in code, blocks the network entirely, and runs a command in a sandboxed child while the parent stays free, with `enforcement_mode="seccomp"`, which layers a static seccomp filter under Landlock so that even the socket types Landlock doesn't cover are denied:

```python
caps = CapabilitySet()
caps.allow_path(str(HERE / "workspace"), AccessMode.READ_WRITE)
caps.allow_path(str(HERE / "goose"), AccessMode.READ_WRITE)
for system in ("/usr", "/lib", "/lib64", "/etc", str(Path.home() / ".local" / "bin")):
    if Path(system).exists():
        caps.allow_path(system, AccessMode.READ)
caps.block_network()

result = sandboxed_exec(caps, command, cwd=str(HERE), timeout_secs=args.timeout,
                        env=child_environment(), inherit_env=False,
                        enforcement_mode=args.mode)
```

```bash
uv run python nono_agent.py -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
```

```console
cat: decoys/.aws/credentials: Permission denied
```

```bash
uv run python nono_agent.py -- curl -sS --max-time 5 https://example.com/
```

```console
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com
```

Same `curl: (6)` as the first lab's seccomp filter, from the opposite direction: that filter said no to a syscall number, and this sandbox says the destination was never there.

## Cleanup

_~2 min · Hands-on_

Stop the containers and remove the profile and outputs:

```bash
docker compose --profile obi down -v
rm -f ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
rm -rf policies/rendered
rm -f tetra.out tetra-enforce.out agent-enforce.out agent-override.out agent-nono.out agent-nono-profile.out collector.log obi.log dry-run.txt
```

```console
$ docker compose --profile obi down -v
$ rm -f ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
$ rm -rf policies/rendered
$ rm -f tetra.out tetra-enforce.out agent-enforce.out agent-override.out agent-nono.out agent-nono-profile.out collector.log obi.log dry-run.txt
```
